h-13.3-manage-outputs.title: 13.3 Manage Stakeholder Engagement (continued): ground rules, meeting types, outputs
h-13.3-manage-outputs.notes: Ground rules, defined in the team charter, set expected behaviour of team members and other stakeholders regarding stakeholder engagement. Meetings: decision making, issue resolution, lessons learned and retrospectives, project kick-off, sprint planning, status updates. Outputs: change requests (changes to project or product scope may emerge; processed via 4.6); plan updates (communications management plan - new or changed stakeholder requirements; stakeholder engagement plan - new or changed strategies); document updates (change log, issue log, lessons learned, stakeholder register - new information provided to stakeholders about resolved issues, approved changes and status).

h-13.4-monitor-engagement.title: 13.4 Monitor Stakeholder Engagement: analysis, decision making, engagement matrix tracking, communication and interpersonal skills, outputs
h-13.4-monitor-engagement.notes: Monitor stakeholder relationships and tailor engagement strategies by modifying strategies and plans; key benefit: maintains or increases the efficiency and effectiveness of engagement as the project and environment change; performed throughout. Inputs: plan (resource management plan - team management methods; communications management plan; stakeholder engagement plan); documents (issue log, lessons learned, project communications distributed, risk register - incl. stakeholder-related risks, stakeholder register - identification, assessment, classification); work performance data (which stakeholders are supportive, level and type of engagement); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance, personnel policies, stakeholder risk thresholds, channels, trends, geography); OPAs (social media, ethics, security; issue, risk, change, data management; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical information). Tools: data analysis - alternatives analysis (options to respond to variances in desired engagement), root cause analysis (why engagement isn't having the planned effect), stakeholder analysis (positions of groups and individuals at any time); decision making - multicriteria decision analysis (prioritised, weighted criteria for successful engagement), voting (choose the best response to an engagement variance); data representation - stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (tracks changes in each stakeholder's engagement level); communication skills - feedback (ensure information is received and understood), presentations; interpersonal skills - active listening, cultural awareness, leadership (communicate the vision and inspire support), networking (access to information on engagement levels), political awareness; meetings (status meetings, standups, retrospectives, others agreed in the engagement plan; face-to-face is ideal but expensive - technology bridges the gap). Outputs: work performance information (status of engagement - current support vs desired levels in the engagement assessment matrix, stakeholder cube or other tool); change requests (corrective and preventive actions to improve engagement); plan updates (resource management plan - team responsibilities for engagement; communications management plan; stakeholder engagement plan); document updates (issue log - indicates attitudes, lessons learned, risk register - responses to stakeholder risks, stakeholder register). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

std-intro-and-projects.title: The Standard for Project Management: purpose and relationship to the Guide; projects and project management; competing constraints
std-intro-and-projects.notes: Part 2 is The Standard for Project Management (ANSI/PMI 99-001-2017). A standard is a document established by an authority, custom or general consent as a model or example; developed on consensus, openness, due process and balance; describes processes considered good practice on most projects most of the time, organised by Process Group; defines key concepts (relationship to strategy and objectives, governance, portfolio and program management, project environment, success), life cycles, stakeholders and the PM's role. Section 1 gives key concepts; Sections 2-6 define each Process Group and describe its processes with key benefits, inputs and outputs (tools and techniques are left to the Guide). The Standard is the foundation and framework for the Guide, which adds context, environment, influences, ITTO descriptions, tools and techniques, key concepts and trends per Knowledge Area. 1.1: a project is a temporary endeavour to create a unique product, service or result; temporary means a definite beginning and end, not necessarily short; ends when objectives are achieved, or it is terminated because objectives will not or cannot be met or the need no longer exists; termination requires approval by an appropriate authority (a point stated in the Standard). Project management = applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to meet requirements, through applying and integrating the processes. Managing a project typically includes identifying requirements; addressing stakeholders' needs, concerns and expectations; active communication; managing resources; balancing competing constraints - scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources and risk. Circumstances influence how processes are implemented and constraints prioritised.

std-ppp-governance-success.title: Standard: portfolios, programs and projects; OPM as a strategy execution framework; organisational vs project governance; project success and benefits management
std-ppp-governance-success.notes: 1.2: portfolio = projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios and operations managed in a coordinated manner to achieve strategic objectives; portfolio management = centralised management of one or more portfolios, ensuring performance consistent with objectives and optimising resource allocation; may include operational work. Program = related projects, subsidiary programs and program activities managed in a coordinated manner for benefits not otherwise available; includes program-related work outside discrete projects and possibly operational work; program management supports strategy by authorising, changing or terminating projects and managing interdependencies: resolving resource constraints and conflicts, aligning with strategy, managing issues and change in shared governance, addressing risks affecting components, managing benefits realisation by analysing, sequencing and monitoring interdependencies. A project can be stand-alone, within a program or within a portfolio. Figure 1-1: strategy drives portfolios, programs and projects with shared resources and stakeholders; relationships are not always strictly hierarchical. OPM is described here as a strategy execution framework using portfolio, program and project management to deliver strategy consistently and predictably for better performance, results and sustainable competitive advantage. 1.3: types of governance - organisational, OPM, portfolio, program, project. Organisational governance = structured direction and control through policies and processes to meet strategic and operational goals, typically by a board of directors for accountability, fairness and transparency; it influences lower levels by enforcing legal, regulatory, standards and compliance requirements, defining ethical, social and environmental responsibilities and specifying operational, legal and risk policies. Project governance = framework, functions and processes guiding project management activities; at project level: guiding and overseeing work, ensuring adherence to policies and standards, establishing governance roles, responsibilities and authorities, decisions on risk escalations, changes and resources, ensuring stakeholder engagement, monitoring performance. Project governance framework elements: stage gate or phase reviews; identifying, escalating and resolving risks and issues; roles, responsibilities and authorities; knowledge management and lessons learned; decision making, problem solving and escalation beyond the PM's authority; reviewing and approving project and product changes beyond the PM's authority. 1.4: projects realise business opportunities aligned with strategy; a business case often precedes initiation (objectives, investment, financial and qualitative success criteria) and is the basis for measuring success. Strategic considerations initiating projects: market demand, strategic opportunity/business need, social need, environmental consideration, customer request, technological advancement, legal or regulatory requirement, existing or forecasted problem. Benefits management plan: target benefits, strategic alignment, timeframe, benefits owner, metrics, risks. Success is measured against objectives and success criteria; product success (market share, operating cost, new product success) may only be known after transition, so the PMO, portfolio steering committee or another business function evaluates later. Business case and benefits management plan are developed before initiation and referenced after completion, so they are business documents - not project documents or plan components - though they may be inputs (e.g., to Develop Project Charter).

std-life-cycle-stakeholders-pm.title: Standard: project life cycle and phases, impact of variables over time, stakeholders, role of the project manager, Knowledge Areas
std-life-cycle-stakeholders-pm.notes: 1.5: life cycle = series of phases from start to completion; phase = logically related activities culminating in deliverables; sequential, iterative or overlapping; names, number and duration set by management and control needs, nature of the project and application area; phases are time bound with a control point (phase review, phase gate, control gate) where the charter and business documents are re-examined and performance compared to the plan to decide whether to change, terminate or continue. Influenced by organisation, industry, development method or technology. Generic structure (Figure 1-2): starting the project, organizing and preparing, carrying out the work, closing (labelled 'ending') the project. Generic characteristics (Figure 1-3): cost and staffing low at the start, rise during the work and drop rapidly near closure; risk greatest at the start and decreasing as decisions are made and deliverables accepted; stakeholders' ability to influence the product's final characteristics without significant cost or schedule impact is highest at the start and decreases; the cost of making changes and correcting errors increases substantially toward completion. 1.6: stakeholder = individual, group or organisation that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity or outcome; internal or external; actively involved, passively involved or unaware; positive or negative impact. Internal examples: sponsor, resource manager, PMO, portfolio steering committee, program manager, other PMs, team members; external: customers, end users, suppliers, shareholders, regulatory bodies, competitors (Figure 1-4 mirrors the sphere of influence figure). Involvement ranges from surveys and focus groups to full sponsorship and changes over the life cycle, so identification, analysis, engagement and expectation management throughout are critical. 1.7: the PM is assigned by the performing organisation to lead the team; reporting relationships follow structure and governance; attributes: knowledge (PM, business environment, technical), skills (lead, coordinate, collaborate, solve problems, decide), abilities (develop and manage scope, schedules, budgets, resources, risks, plans, presentations, reports), other attributes (personality, attitude, ethics, leadership). Interpersonal skills: leadership, team building, motivating, communicating, influencing, decision making, political and cultural awareness, negotiating, facilitating, managing conflict, coaching. Success = objectives achieved plus stakeholder satisfaction; tailor approach, life cycle and processes. 1.8: Knowledge Areas are fields or areas of specialisation commonly employed; a Knowledge Area is a set of processes associated with a topic; ten used on most projects most of the time, others may be needed; definitions repeat Part 1 Section 1.2.4.6.
